paragraphs.text: This [Lapsang Souchong](lapsang:definition) comes from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), on the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. The range makes two very different teas on different ground: rock oolong in the lower valleys and cliffs, and Lapsang on the high, forested northern edge around [Tongmu](wuyi-mountains:two-teas), the village widely called the birthplace of Chinese black tea. Tea shipped from this area to Europe in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was sold as [Bohea](fujian:history), a spelling of the local name for Wuyi.

It is a [red tea](red:definition), the fully oxidised tea English calls black, and Lapsang is called the oldest of them, though the dates given for its beginning differ. The leaf is withered, rolled and left to oxidise in covered baskets, then passed through a [hot pan](lapsang:making) to stop the oxidation quickly and rolled again while hot, which shapes the strip and helps it take up smoke. In the traditional way it is dried over a [pine fire](lapsang:smoke) in a qinglou, a wooden house of several floors with the fire at the bottom and the leaf on bamboo mats above, so the heat rises through it.

brewing.text: In a cup or pot, use about 3 grams for 240 ml, with water at 90 to 100°C, and steep about two to five minutes, usually around three. Gongfu style, use about 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan or pot, with short steeps that grow a little longer each round. Too hot or too long and the smoke turns harsh and bitter and covers the tea.

notice.text: In the smoked tea: pine and pine resin, longan or dried longan, campfire or woodsmoke, dried fruit and a sweet aftertaste. In the unsmoked tea: honey, longan and fruit or flowers.
